DRAC Primer Session 2026 Introduction Welcome to the Canadian Bioinformatics Workshops (CBW) DRAC Primer Session. This hands-on course introduces a shared high-performance computing (HPC) training cluster and the commands needed to run reproducible bioinformatics analyses. You will learn how to connect, manage files, transfer data, use software, submit and monitor Slurm jobs, and access interactive computing resources. The workshop finishes with a short bioinformatics challenge. Slides Please find below the slides for this session. Workshop Details Date: Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Audience: CBW participants who are new to Linux or HPC. Platform: DRAC-hosted CBW training cluster. The instructors will provide the registration link and workshop credentials; do not post passwords in shared documents. Before the session Bring a laptop with a working internet connection and an SSH client (Terminal on macOS/Linux, or Windows Terminal/PowerShell with OpenSSH). Open the link https://mokey.cbw.c3.ca, and register your username, password and email address as instructed. This session targets the beginners who has little experience in command line, linux, and HPC. The login host for this workshop is @cbw.c3.ca; do not use a personal DRAC cluster account unless instructed. Use the workshop-specific instructions rather than assumptions about other DRAC clusters. Course Outline Date: Wednesday, October 28, 2026 Time: 11:00–15:00 PDT Time (PDT) Module / Activity 11:00–11:35 Module 1: HPC Infrastructure, registration and login 11:35–12:10 Module 2: Working with directories and files 12:10–12:20 Break 12:20–12:50 Module 3: Software environments and reproducibility 12:50–13:35 Module 4: Submit and monitor jobs with Slurm 13:35–13:45 Break 13:45–14:50 Module 5: Bioinformatics Mini-Challenge 14:50–15:00 Questions and Wrap-up The session also includes instructor-led demonstrations, exercises and breaks. Module 1 - HPC infrastructure, registration and login Learning goals By the end of this module, you should be able to describe a training cluster, register for the workshop, and connect through SSH. What is HPC? High-performance computing (HPC) joins computing nodes, fast networking, shared storage, and a workload scheduler to support workloads that are too large or slow for a single laptop. Component Purpose Login node SSH access, lightweight editing, compilation, job submission Compute node CPU and memory resources for running analyses Slurm Queues, allocates and monitors jobs Shared storage Stores data accessible to jobs Local node storage Temporary space used during a job, when configured Typical workflow HPC Cluster Your computer | | SSH v +-------------+ | Login Node | +-------------+ | | Submit jobs v Slurm | +-------------------------+ | | | v v v +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | Compute | | Compute | | Compute | | Node 1 | | Node 2 | | Node 3 | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ \ | / \ | / +---------------------+ | Shared Storage | +---------------------+ Important: Do not run computationally intensive analyses on login nodes. Submit batch jobs or request interactive allocations. HPC terminology CPU core: unit of CPU computation requested by a job. Memory (RAM): memory required while a job runs. Wall time: maximum elapsed run time requested. Job: work the scheduler executes with an allocated resource request. Partition: scheduling queue or resource grouping (available partitions vary). Register for the workshop Open the https://mokey.cbw.c3.ca and click on Create Account. Register the required username, first name, last name, password and email. The password must be at least 8 characters. Keep your credentials private. Use the workshop account, which may be distinct from a regular DRAC account. Connect by SSH Open Terminal (macOS/Linux) or Windows Terminal / PowerShell: ssh YOUR_USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca Replace YOUR_USERNAME with the username you registered. Confirm the host key only after verifying the hostname with the instructors, then enter your password when prompted. The password is not shown as you type. Verify where you are: whoami hostname pwd To disconnect: exit Exercise: first login Connect to cbw.c3.ca. Run whoami, hostname, and pwd. Identify which machine you are on and why intensive computation belongs on compute nodes. Check your understanding whoami prints your login name; hostname prints the machine name; pwd prints your current directory. Exact values depend on your account and the current training infrastructure. Common connection issues Permission denied: Confirm the username and workshop password; do not share credentials. Could not resolve hostname: Check that cbw.c3.ca was entered correctly and that your network can resolve it. Connection timed out: Check connectivity or ask the instructor whether network access is restricted. Backup solution: open jupyter.cbw.c3.ca in your browser login with your username and password Select Terminal in User Interface click on logout to exit. Module 2: Working with directories and files Learning goals Navigate Linux directories, inspect text files, organize results, and transfer files between your computer and the training cluster. Explore the directory pwd # Where am I? ls # What is here? ls -lh # Include modified dates, file sizes, etc. mkdir -p cbw-primer # Make a direcotory / make a folder cd cbw-primer # Navigate into the folder cd .. # Go to the parent folder (move one level up) pwd cd .. # Now in /home pwd cd .. # Now in / pwd cd .. pwd ls -lh cd project # Now in /project pwd cd /home/USERNAME # Replace USERNAME with your own username. Equivalent to: cd ~ pwd cd ../../project # Go back to /project with relative path pwd cd - # Go to the previous directory pwd # /home/USERNAME Important: Use _ to replace space in file or folder name. Paths beginning with / are absolute; paths relative to your working directory are relative. .. refers to the parent directory and ~ refers to your home directory. Create and inspect files cd /home/USERNAME/cbw-primer printf 'sample	reads
A	12
B	8
' > counts.tsv cat counts.tsv head -n 2 counts.tsv wc -l counts.tsv cp counts.tsv counts-copy.tsv mv counts-copy.tsv counts-backup.tsv > creates or overwrites a file. Use it carefully. Use >> to append. printf 'C	15
' >> counts.tsv cat counts.tsv You can use nano counts.tsv to edit the file. Cheat sheet: https://www.nano-editor.org/dist/latest/cheatsheet.html File transfer from your own computer Run the following commands in a separate terminal on your laptop, not inside the cluster SSH session: # Download a result from the cluster rsync -avh USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca:/home/USERNAME/cbw-primer/counts.tsv ./ # Upload one local file to your cluster home directory rsync -avh ./counts.tsv USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca:/scratch/USERNAME Change USERNAME and local paths as needed. rsync works over SSH and can resume incremental transfers. FileZilla is a graphical alternative: select SFTP, host cbw.c3.ca, port 22, and use your assigned workshop credentials. Exercise Create /home/USERNAME/cbw-primer/results and navigate into it. Create a text file samples.txt, then inspect it with cat and wc -l. Upload a small text file from your laptop using rsync or FileZilla. Download the file back to your laptop. Example commands mkdir -p /home/USERNAME/cbw-primer/results cd /home/USERNAME/cbw-primer/results printf 'sample1
sample2
sample3
' > ~/cbw-primer/samples.txt cat samples.txt wc -l ~/cbw-primer/samples.txt From your laptop: rsync -avh USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca:/home/USERNAME/cbw-primer/results/counts.tsv ./ Shared filesystem etiquette Use descriptive filenames. Avoid generating millions of tiny files or copying large datasets unnecessarily. Ask instructors which directories are appropriate for persistent data and temporary job output; filesystem paths and quotas are cluster-specific. Next: Module 3. Module 3. Software environments and reproducibility Learning goals Find available software, load an environment module, and identify the commands and versions used in an analysis. Environment modules Clusters provide software through environment modules. Available applications and versions depend on the training system. module avail module list module spider python # Available on systems using Lmod module load python # If an appropriate Python module is available python --version module list module load modifies your environment (for example PATH) for the current shell. When finished, you can use module unload <module-name> or module reset. Python virtual environments If Python and the venv module are available: virtualenv --no-download ~/cbw-primer/venv source ~/cbw-primer/venv/bin/activate python --version which python pip install --no-index emoji pip list python -c 'import emoji;print(emoji.emojize(":elephant:"))' deactivate python -c 'import emoji;print(emoji.emojize(":elephant:"))' For those who would like to use Conda: Create a definition file, e.g. alignment.def and edit as needed: Bootstrap: docker From: ubuntu:22.04 Stage: build %environment export LC_ALL=C source /usr/local/miniconda3/bin/activate alignment %post apt update && apt install -y wget mkdir /conda cd /conda wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh -O miniconda.sh bash miniconda.sh -b -u -p /usr/local/miniconda3 rm miniconda.sh export PATH="/usr/local/miniconda3/bin":$PATH eval "$(/usr/local/miniconda3/bin/conda shell.bash hook)" conda tos accept --override-channels --channel https://repo.anaconda.com/pkgs/main conda tos accept --override-channels --channel https://repo.anaconda.com/pkgs/r conda create -y -n alignment conda activate alignment conda install -n alignment -y bioconda::bwa rm -rf /conda Create the container image, which is called singularity container image file (sif): module load apptainer apptainer build allignment.sif allignment.def Run the software built in the container: module load apptainer apptainer exec alignment.sif bwa -h Exercise Find the latest version of SPAdes installed and load the module. Find the installation path of loaded SPAdes. Install numpy in venv. Next: Module 4. Submit and monitor jobs with Slurm

Module 4. Submit and monitor jobs with Slurm Why use a scheduler? Write a batch script Understand resource requests Monitor and diagnose jobs Interactive allocations Exercise

Module 4. Submit and monitor jobs with Slurm Why use a scheduler? On HPC, computation is submitted as a job. Slurm reserves cores, memory and time, and executes the job on an allocated compute node rather than on the login node. Write a batch script Create hello.sbatch with nano hello.sbatch and enter: #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=hello-hpc #SBATCH --account=def-sponsor00 #SBATCH --time=00:05:00 #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --ntasks=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1 #SBATCH --mem=1000M set -euo pipefail printf 'Host: %s
' "$(hostname)" printf 'Job: %s
' "$SLURM_JOB_ID" printf 'CPUs: %s
' "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" sleep 10 printf 'Finished
' Submit and inspect: sbatch hello.sbatch sq sacct --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ExitCode,NodeList cat slurm_JOB_ID.out Replace JOB_ID with the ID returned by sbatch. sacct reporting can lag and depends on the cluster’s accounting configuration. Understand resource requests Slurm Option Description Analogy (Restaurant) --time Maximum wall-clock time for the job Time allowed to prepare an order --ntasks Number of tasks/processes Number of dishes being prepared simultaneously in an order --nodes Number of compute nodes Number of kitchens --cpus-per-task Number of CPU cores per task Number of chefs working on each dish --mem Memory allocated per node Available workspace in each kitchen Request resources based on measured usage instead of reserving much more than necessary. A job may remain PENDING while resources are unavailable. Monitor and diagnose jobs sq sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ReqTRES%60 scancel JOB_ID # Only when you intend to cancel the job seff JOB_ID # Display the utilization If you see OUT_OF_MEMORY or a time-limit failure, inspect logs and resource requests before rerunning. Interactive allocations salloc For short tests and troubleshooting, request an interactive allocation: salloc --time=00:15:00 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=1G srun --pty bash hostname htop # Press "q" to quit echo $SLURM_TMPDIR # Display the path to local temporary storage exit # Exit the compute-node shell exit # Release the allocation The first exit closes the interactive shell on the compute node. The second exit leaves the allocation shell and releases the Slurm allocation. JupyterHub Open the workshop JupyterHub in your browser and follow the organizer’s instructions. A typical workflow is: Sign in with your workshop credentials. Select an available compute profile, if prompted. Launch a notebook or terminal. Shut down your session when finished. Exercise Submit a new job which runs the following command: timeout 120s bash -c 'x=$(head -c 250M /dev/zero | tr "\0" x); sleep 120' find its job ID, inspect its output log, and report whether the job completed successfully. module-5.-bioinformatics-mini-challenge.html

Module 5. Bioinformatics Mini-Challenge Goal 1: Create a sample FASTA file 2: Explore the data 3: Build a simple analysis script 4: Submit the analysis to Slurm 5: Save and transfer results 6: Stretch challenge 7. Best practices Wrap-up

Module 5. Bioinformatics Mini-Challenge Goal Combine shell operations, a small sequence dataset, a reproducible script and a Slurm batch job. All data are generated inside your workspace; no external downloads are required. 1: Create a sample FASTA file mkdir -p ~/cbw-primer/challenge cd ~/cbw-primer/challenge cat > sequences.fa <<'EOF' >seqA ACGTACGT >seqB GGGTTT >seqC ATATATATAT EOF FASTA records begin with > followed by an identifier and one or more sequence lines. 2: Explore the data head sequences.fa grep -c '^>' sequences.fa wc -l sequences.fa Question: How many sequences are present? Can I use wc -l then devided by 2 to count the number of sequences? Answer There are 3 sequences. FASTA sequences can occupy multiple lines, so counting total lines does not count records reliably. Counting header lines beginning with > is appropriate for well-formed FASTA. 3: Build a simple analysis script Save the following as analyze.sh: #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail input="${1:?Usage: bash analyze.sh INPUT.fa}" printf 'Input: %s\n' "$input" printf 'Sequences: ' grep -c '^>' "$input" printf 'Total bases: ' awk '!/^>/ {gsub(/[[:space:]]/, ""); n += length($0)} END {print n+0}' "$input" Run it: bash analyze.sh sequences.fa Expected results: 3 sequences and 24 bases. The base count sums sequence-line lengths and supports wrapped FASTA records. 4: Submit the analysis to Slurm Save as analyze.sbatch: #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --account=def-sponsor00 #SBATCH --job-name=fasta-count #SBATCH --time=00:05:00 #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --ntasks=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1 #SBATCH --mem=1000M set -euo pipefail cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR" bash analyze.sh sequences.fa Run: sbatch analyze.sbatch sq Once it finishes, inspect the slurm-JOBID.out file (replace JOBID with the actual number). 5: Save and transfer results From your laptop, retrieve the output with rsync (substitute the job ID and workshop username): rsync -avh YOUR_USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca:~/cbw-primer/challenge/slurm-JOBID.out ./ 6: Stretch challenge Modify analyze.sh to accept multiple FASTA files, using a for filename in "$@" loop. Consider how you would process hundreds of files using a Slurm job array rather than running one long serial task. 7. Best practices Do NOT run the entire workflow in a single job!!!!!! Estimate the walltime, RAM, CPUs etc by benchmarking the tools Find the bottleneck of the tool Avoid duplicating the large public dataset such as NCBI BLAST database, Kraken2, Alphafold3, ColabFold, gnomAD ete, which might be found at: /cvmfs/bio.data.computecanada.ca Understand the pros/cons of different file systems, such as $SLURM_TMPDIR, /scratch, /project, /home, /nearline Wrap-up You have registered and logged in to an HPC training cluster, organized data, used environment modules, submitted and inspected a job, and run a reproducible bioinformatics script. For production work, benchmark resource usage and use the official cluster documentation and policies.
